awd_titl_txt: STTR Phase I: Bioabsorbable Magnesium with a Tailorable Absorption Profile for Maxillofacial Fixation
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impacts and commercial potential of this Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project lie in developing a magnesium (Mg) alloy for implants that support healing by temporarily fixating bones or stabilizing tissues. These implants provide mechanical support during recovery and are gradually absorbed by the body, restoring the implant site without requiring removal surgeries. Specifically, this project will develop a bioabsorbable magnesium alloy for maxillofacial fixation. This innovation aims to improve healthcare outcomes by eliminating secondary hardware removal surgeries, which occur in 5-20% of maxillofacial fixation cases and cost the U.S. healthcare system $1.72 billion annually. Permanent metal implants often lead to ongoing risks and expenses, while resorbable polymers, an alternative, are limited by limited strength, unreliable healing, and complex surgical procedures. A bioabsorbable metal implant with superior mechanical robustness and controlled absorption addresses these challenges and offers the potential to capture market share from both titanium and polymer implants. With 19% of the maxillofacial fixation market already using resorbable polymers, a superior bioabsorbable alloy would significantly improve clinical outcomes while reducing healthcare costs.

This Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project will demonstrate the feasibility of a bioabsorbable alloy with a customizable absorption profile tailored for maxillofacial fixation. Intellectual merit includes (1) developing a bioabsorbable alloy with tunable absorption profiles, (2) understanding how processing affects absorption behavior, and (3) validating a large-animal preclinical model for novel bioabsorbable implants. Technical challenges addressed in this project include the impact of processing on microstructure and absorption (TC1), correlation between in vitro and in vivo absorption profiles (TC2), anatomical variations in absorption (TC3), absorption effects on the bone-implant interface (TC4), and gas evolution's impact on bone density (TC5).

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF STTR Phase I project evaluated the feasibility of Curasorb, a bioabsorbable magnesium (Mg) alloy, for maxillofacial fixation. Bioabsorbable magnesium alloy implants are designed to provide mechanical support during healing and then gradually absorb, restoring the implant site without requiring removal surgery. Current fixation devices are typically made from permanent metals that may remain in the body indefinitely or require secondary removal procedures in some patients, while existing absorbable polymer systems can be limited by reduced mechanical strength, unreliable healing, and complex surgical procedures. The project investigated whether a bioabsorbable magnesium alloy with a tunable absorption profile could be developed, how manufacturing processes influence absorption behavior, and whether a large-animal preclinical model could be used to evaluate bioabsorbable implants across multiple craniofacial anatomies. The long-term goal of this technology is to develop a bioabsorbable fixation system that supports healing and then absorbs after its clinical function is complete, potentially reducing secondary implant-removal procedures and their associated healthcare costs, recovery time, and patient burden.

The project demonstrated that alloy composition and processing can be used to generate distinct absorption profiles and that laboratory corrosion testing can provide useful information for predicting implant absorption behavior in vivo. A major outcome of the project was the development and execution of a large-animal preclinical model used to assess bioabsorbable implants across multiple craniofacial anatomies, including the mandible, maxilla, frontal bone, and zygoma. The study generated data on implant absorption, local tissue response, and bone-to-implant contact over time, while also demonstrating the utility of the model for evaluating and comparing multiple alloy conditions. One important finding was that favorable implant integration was strongly associated with controlled and consistent absorption behavior. Favorable bone-to-implant contact and progressive bone remodeling were observed. Knowledge gained during the study was used to develop next-generation alloy iterations with improved mechanical properties and more controlled absorption behavior, providing a clear path for continued bioabsorbable magnesium technology development. Together, these results improved understanding of how alloy design influences absorption behavior and biological response.

Broader impacts of this work include advancing scientific understanding of bioabsorbable metallic biomaterials and establishing methods that can support development of future absorbable implant technologies. The project generated knowledge related to magnesium alloy composition, manufacturing processes, absorption behavior, osseointegration, and bone remodeling that will guide development of future bioabsorbable implant technologies for orthopedic applications with different healing requirements. The large-animal craniofacial model developed during this work also provides a framework for evaluating such technologies in clinically relevant anatomical locations.

The outcomes of this NSF Phase I project demonstrated the feasibility of a bioabsorbable magnesium alloy with tunable absorption behavior for maxillofacial fixation. The findings showed that alloy design and processing can be used to control absorption behavior while maintaining favorable bone-to-implant contact and supporting bone remodeling. These results establish the technical merit and feasibility of a bioabsorbable metallic fixation platform that supports healing, absorbs after its clinical function is complete, and enables restoration of native bone.
